name: threefold death

attributes.attribute: ritual of stabbing, burning, and drowning
wounded then drowned in a vat of wine

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The threefold death is a Celtic ritual of sacrificial death with three parts. The usual form is a stabbing, a burning, and a drowning. Another version uses strangling, cutting, and drowning. At times the different forms were shared out among the gods. On the continent the forms of death were tied to the gods. Those devoted to Taranis died by fire. Taranis is the thunder god. Those given to Teutates were drowned. Teutates is the ancestral god. Those who went to Esus were hanged. Esus is the tree god. In Ireland several texts tell of this death. Muircertach Mac Erc was wounded. Then, fleeing his burning dwelling, he fell into a vat of wine and drowned there. The failed king Conaire was wounded too. He was stricken with an unquenchable thirst. Then he was burned alive. A body found in Lindow Bog in Britain showed the same marks. That victim had a noose about the neck. His throat was slashed before he drowned in the bogwater.

okr.objective: Record the threefold death as a Celtic sacrificial rite.
key_results: The rite had three parts, often stabbing, burning, and drowning
Victims of Taranis were burned, of Teutates drowned, of Esus hanged
Muircertach Mac Erc drowned in a vat of wine
The Lindow Man had his throat slashed before drowning
